title: Why Do We Yawn? The Science and Theories
summary: Explore what science knows—and doesn't know—about the ancient reflex of yawning, from brain cooling to contagious group signaling.
evidenceNote: While several physiological theories exist, including brain thermoregulation and group alertness signaling, scholars have proposed around twenty reasons for yawning with little agreement on any single primary cause.

scenes.text: Why can just seeing someone yawn make you do it too?
A yawn is an ancient reflex found across almost all vertebrates, from fish and birds to humans.
During a yawn, muscles around the airway fully stretch, dilating the lungs and throat to three or four times their normal size.
Researchers have proposed about twenty reasons for yawning, but there is little agreement on which one comes first.
One prominent theory suggests yawning acts as a thermoregulatory mechanism to keep the brain cool.
Another hypothesis suggests contagious yawning helps synchronize alertness and sleeping patterns within an animal group.
Though its exact physiological function remains unknown, yawning is controlled by complex neurotransmitters in the brain.
